title: Aunt Jennifer's Tigers
summary: Adrienne Rich's short poem contrasts the bold, free tigers that Aunt Jennifer embroiders with her own timid, burdened life in an oppressive marriage. Her art expresses the freedom she never had and will outlive her.

notes.heading: About the poet
notes.html: Adrienne Rich (1929–2012) was an American poet and essayist whose work is closely associated with feminism and the questioning of power in society and family. This poem is one of her early works.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: Aunt Jennifer stitches a panel showing tigers moving proudly through a green forest. They fear no one. She herself is nervous and weighed down by her marriage. Even after her death she will remain marked by that life, but her tigers will go on, proud and unafraid.

notes.heading: Stanza-wise explanation (paraphrase)
notes.html:
Stanza 1

The tigers on the embroidered screen leap about brightly, golden against the green. They are not afraid of the men standing under the tree; they move with the confident grace of knights.

Stanza 2

The aunt's fingers tremble as she works the wool. Even a light ivory needle feels hard to pull, because the heavy wedding ring given by her husband sits on her hand like a burden.

Stanza 3

When she dies, her frightened hands will still carry the marks of the hardships that ruled her life. The tigers she created, however, will continue to stride on, proud and fearless.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Oppression of women in a male-dominated marriage: the wedding band stands for the control exercised by 'Uncle'.
  • Art as escape and self-expression: the tigers have everything the aunt lacks: courage, freedom and confidence.
  • Permanence of art: the creator dies, the creation survives.
  • Contrast between inner desire and outer reality.

notes.heading: Poetic devices
notes.html:
DeviceWhere it is used
SymbolismTigers = freedom and fearlessness; wedding band = bondage; needle and wool = her only means of expression
ContrastBold tigers against the trembling aunt
AlliterationRepeated consonant sounds, e.g. the 'f' sound describing her fingers, the 'p' sound in the description of the tigers' movement
Transferred epithetThe hands are called frightened, though it is the aunt who is frightened
HyperboleThe ring is described as having enormous weight
Metaphor / imageryThe tigers compared to bright jewels; vivid colour images of gold and green
Rhyme schemeaabb in each stanza (rhyming couplets)

notes.heading: Title and message
notes.html: The title puts the tigers at the centre: they belong to Aunt Jennifer because she made them, and they represent the self she could not be. The poem suggests that a spirit suppressed in life finds a voice in art, and it quietly criticises marriages that crush a woman's individuality.

mcqs.q: The tigers in the poem are
mcqs.explanation: Aunt Jennifer creates them with wool and needle on a screen.
They embody the qualities the aunt longs for.

options: She is burdened by her married life
The needle is made of iron
mcqs.explanation: The difficulty reflects her mental and physical exhaustion under an oppressive marriage.

mcqs.explanation: They are completely unafraid of the men beneath the tree.

questions.q: How do the tigers differ from Aunt Jennifer?
questions.answerHtml: The tigers are bold, energetic and free; they move with pride and fear no man. Aunt Jennifer is timid, nervous and weighed down by her marriage. They are what she wishes to be, so the contrast highlights her suppressed life.

questions.q: What is suggested by the heavy weight of the wedding band?
questions.answerHtml: The ring is not physically heavy; the weight is symbolic. It stands for the duties, restrictions and domination that marriage has placed on Aunt Jennifer, which have drained her confidence and freedom.

questions.q: Why do you think Aunt Jennifer chose to create tigers?
questions.answerHtml: Tigers are powerful and fearless, qualities missing from her own life. By creating them she gives shape to her hidden desire for strength and freedom. Her art becomes a silent protest and an escape.

questions.q: The poem is a comment on gender relations within marriage. Discuss.
questions.answerHtml:
The poem shows a marriage in which the woman has lost her individuality. Aunt Jennifer's fingers tremble; a small needle is hard for her to pull; the ring her husband gave sits on her hand like a load. The husband never appears, yet his control is felt everywhere, which shows how deep it runs.

Against this, the tigers she embroiders are confident and unafraid of men. The contrast tells us that the aunt has the imagination and spirit for freedom but has not been allowed to live it. Even in death her hands will bear the marks of what she endured.

Through one ordinary woman the poet speaks for many women whose identities are reduced to their roles as wives. The poem does not shout; it protests through quiet images, and suggests that creative expression is one way an oppressed spirit survives.

questions.q: 'Art outlives the artist.' Explain with reference to the poem.
questions.answerHtml:
The final stanza looks ahead to the aunt's death. Her body will still carry the signs of a fearful, controlled life: nothing in her personal story changes. Yet the panel she stitched will continue to exist, and on it the tigers will go on moving with pride.

This shows two things. First, art has a permanence that human life lacks. Second, art can hold a truth about the artist that her life could not show. The world saw a submissive wife; the tigers reveal a woman who valued courage and dignity.

So the poem ends on a note that is both sad and hopeful. The aunt could not free herself, but her creation is free, and it carries her real self into the future. In that sense she wins a quiet victory over her circumstances.
